The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 

# Executive Summary What will happen to the market surplus? 







- The cobalt market is currently being impacted by oversupply and slower than expected demand.  Prices of low grade material contracted by 12.3% year-on-year to US$16.44/lb in 2011 and a further 18.5% year-on-year to US$14.43/lb in H1 2012.  CRU forecasts that prices will average US$14.00/lb in full year 2012 due to a combination of refined surplus along with high levels of inventories of raw materials in China.  Looking ahead, we predict that consecutive annual surpluses in the refined market will continue weighing on prices in the medium-term.  It is anticipated that prices will reach a low of US$12.80/lb in 2014, before increasing to US$17.00/lb in 2017, when the refined market is predicted to turn to a deficit. 

- Despite a slower than expected consumption growth in the near-term, we anticipate that demand for refined cobalt will register a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022.  This is largely driven by demand for cobalt oxide used in rechargeable batteries.  Other sectors such as aerospace and advanced engineering are projected to support robust demand growth.  Indeed, cobalt demand patterns are partly a function of advances in new technology and developments in traditional metallurgical sectors.  The use of cobalt by growing and high value added end-use sectors does not mean that this commodity is unaffected by a weaker economic outlook. 

- In addition to rapidly growing volumes, the supply side of the cobalt market has recently become more complicated as an increasing amount of concentrates and intermediates are produced and use

d as feed in the production of refined material, in particular chemicals. CRU estimates that, currently, about 60% of total cobalt units come from mines in the African Copper Belt. Production of intermediate products is registering considerable growth and will be the preferred raw material of refined producers due to higher cobalt content, compared to concentrates, and operational efficiency. Even though demand has been expanding at a CAGR of 6.0% in the last 10 years, capacity additions mainly triggered by copper and nickel projects have added a significant amount of cobalt units, thus putting downward pressure on prices. The above, coupled with macroeconomic challenges, generates a bearish feeling in the cobalt market. Since mid-2011, this negative feeling has been exacerbated by a slowdown in China; nevertheless, cobalt consumption is growing strongly but at a slower rate than projected last year. Benchmark 99.3% prices contracted by 12.3% to US$16.44/lb in 2011. In H1 2012, prices registered further losses to US$14.43/lb, an 18.5% decline from H1 2011. CRU forecasts that prices will average US$14.00/lb in 2012; at the time of writing, 99.3% material was trading below US$13.00/lb. Oversupply concerns have been weighing on prices. We estimate that the refined cobalt market was balanced in 2010 and exhibited a surplus of 2,781 tonnes in 2011. For the current year, we predict that the surplus will fall to 420 tonnes. This is mainly attributed to the fact that small Chinese processors are expected to cut primary production in the current year. However, the predicted fall in the market surplus for 2012 does not imply that the cobalt market will be tighter. This is because there is a significant accumulation of concentrates and intermediates stocks; we estimate that those stocks in China amount to about 17,000 tonnes of cobalt contained. We believe that the raw material stockpile in China is another factor putting downward pressure

on market prices. Those inventories are expected to fall in order to meet a deficit in the raw material market in 2011-2013. In addition, there is evidence from trade statistics that Chinese imports of cobalt feed have recently fallen substantially. While it is more obvious to assess market tightness by looking at the refined market balance, CRU is of the opinion that the cobalt raw material market also has an important role. This is especially relevant for by-products, as mine output does not necessarily respond to the needs of the final market. ###### Oversupply has been putting pressure on prices since 2010 US$/lb

CRU International Limited confidential The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 Executive Summary 3 ###### Future market: Supply shortages are expected in the long-term The current oversupply concerns extend to the medium-term as well. While refined demand is anticipated to expand at a CAGR of 6.8% in 2012-2017, supply growth is expected to be faster. Taking a conservative approach in our supply forecasts, we predict that the refined cobalt market will see consecutive annual surpluses in 2013-2016. We believe that the refined market surplus will reach 4,173 tonnes in 2014; benchmark prices are predicted to contract to US$12.80/lb in that year. The refined market is projected to turn to a deficit in 2017; prices are forecast to increase to US$17.00/lb. CRU would like to emphasise the fact that our refined production forecasts are backed by sufficient supply of raw materials. Our detailed raw material supply projection out to 2017 shows that there will be sufficient feed to support refined production. In fact, due to significant capacity additions of intermediate products, total raw material supply growth is expected to be enough in order to meet refined production needs out to 2017. CRU believes that raw material supply growth will be mainly a result of robust growth in the supply of intermediate products, rather than concentrates. It is anticipated that the supply of concentrates will fall. The DRC intends to process concentrates domestically, in order to capture the value added and export feed in the form of intermediates. This trend is justified by recent trade statistics and CRU believes that it will continue in the medium-term. However, the cobalt market is anticipated to see a turning point in the long-run. With demand expected to continue growing robustly, we believe that there is going to be a shortage of cobalt units. Even though in the near/medium-term the cobalt market is expected to be oversupplied mainly due to significant copper/nickel-triggered capacity additions, the picture changes dramatically in the longterm. Looking

at the potential of new projects, we understand that the outlook for further additions is uncertain.  From what we identify as active new projects, 75% of them are still at the exploration and development stage.  Medium-term oversupply concerns and low current prices have affected the development of new projects.  This has also been impacted by a weak macroeconomic environment. 

A long-term shortage of cobalt units is based on the prediction that refined demand will have grown at a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022.  This growth rate is largely a function of consumption trends, especially in the critical field of rechargeable batteries.  As the size of the total cobalt market grows, the additional quantity demanded each year by end-use sectors increases as well.  For instance, in the period 2001-2010, demand for refined cobalt grew at an average of 3,228 tonnes per annum. However, according to CRU’s projections the equivalent volume in 2011-2020 is anticipated to soar to 6,021 tonnes.  In practice this is about the size of one project alone.  New capacity may come from a variety of operations; importantly, the sources of finance as well as the degree of risk aversion for each project can vary significantly.  The above factors will drive the long-term price of cobalt.

The Outlook for Cobalt 2012     Executive Summary 

###### Demand: Robust growth anticipated in the medium/long-term 

Refined cobalt consumption continued to grow robustly in 2011, registering a 5.9% year-on-year increase to 77,015 tonnes.  That was a return to long-term growth rates, down from a 13.9% expansion in 2010.  Our estimates suggest that cobalt demand growth is strong and consistently outperforms advances in the global industrial production index. 

Demand from chemical sectors reached 44,150 tonnes in 2011, a 6.3% increase from the previous year.  That was primarily driven by cobalt oxide used in lithium ion battery cells.  It was also supported by demand for cobalt oxide, which is used in the manufacture of PET.  CRU introduced a new end-use sector for cobalt sulphate; we identified that copper production used 471 tonnes of cobalt contained in 2011.  Demand from metallurgical sectors rose by 5.3% year-on-year to 32,865 tonnes in 2011.  Cobalt used in cemented carbides and rotating components for aircraft engines saw strong growth, boosted by healthy demand from the engineering and aerospace sectors respectively. 

It is anticipated that refined cobalt cons

umption will increase by 5.9% year-on-year to 81,554 tonnes in 2012. Despite a weaker than previously expected economic outlook, CRU believes that demand for cobalt will benefit from high value added and growing end-use sectors. Expanding markets such as batteries for high-end electronic devices and EV/HEV, the aerospace industry, and advanced engineering are projected to keep fuelling the strong demand momentum in the short/medium and long-term. Our consumption forecasts suggest that refined cobalt demand will register a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022, reaching 149,423 tonnes by 2022. Long-term consumption trends show that the Asian cobalt consumption share is expanding rapidly. Considering that Asian demand growth is mainly driven by chemical consumption, we believe that Asia, in particular China, is gaining the new cobalt market share established by cutting-edge technologies. Traditional metallurgical sectors are predicted to maintain a considerable share in industrialised regions; however, this is gradually growing in developing regions too, supported by supply chain trends of end-use sectors, production migration, and transfer of technology. ###### Cobalt demand exhibits a robust long-term growth pattern tonnes

CRU estimates that mine production amounted to 97,003 tonnes cobalt contained in 2011, 60% of which originated from the African Copper Belt. A total of 14 identified operations in the DRC produced ore and concentrate, most of which was exported as feed. Production of intermediate products totalled 35,456 tonnes in 2011; we expect that production of cobalt intermediates will reach 69,230 tonnes by 2017, replacing concentrate as feed in refined cobalt production. Major nickel and copper operations that do not produce refined cobalt metal will contribute to that growth. Intermediates will be the raw material of choice for refined producers due to higher cobalt content than concentrates, as well as logistical and processing efficiency. Total refined supply reached 79,796 tonnes in 2011, twice as high the level in 2000. Chemical products totalled 45,476 tonnes in 2011, primarily using cobalt units from the DRC. Production of refined chemicals is dominated by OMG, Chinese processors and the Yabulu refinery. We believe that small C

hinese processors are cutting production in 2012, impacted by low prices and a demand slowdown.  Looking ahead, it is anticipated that large-scale refiners will capture that loss, benefiting from lower processing costs.  CRU projects that refined supply will amount to 111,867 tonnes by 2017; secondary cobalt supply from recycling (Umicore) is expected to gain momentum. 

This year, we present our production cost estimates based on the specific costs of producing cobalt. Half of forecast cobalt production in 2017 will be produced at around US$3.0/lb or below.  This will come from nickel refineries and integrated metal producers.  A considerable refined volume will be produced in the form of hydrometallurgical intermediates, at a cost of US$5.0-8.0/lb.  At operations where cobalt is produced as a main product, costs will be in the range of US$9.0-15.0/lb.  The top of the cost curve will be formed by refined chemical producers in China.  Indeed, Chinese processors that mainly use purchased hydrometallurgical intermediates as their feed will see costs of US$16.4020.80/lb, due to high-cost raw materials.

The Outlook for Cobalt 2012     Executive Summary 

###### Upside risks to the price outlook 

**Stronger than anticipated industrial and economic outlook.** A stronger than expected industrial production activity will favour cobalt consumption.  That will support several end-uses that consume superalloys.  However, given the current economic outlook, the risks are mainly on the dow

nside. A stronger than expected world economic activity will accelerate urbanisation trends, thus boosting the markets for high-end electronics and air travel. **Favourable end-use technology developments that require a higher cobalt intensity of use.** Examples include the emergence of tablets or a potential new end-use sector consuming rechargeable batteries; interestingly, robust growth of mobile phones and laptops significantly boosted cobalt consumption over the last 10 years. **Delays in the start-up or ramp-up of new cobalt metal projects.** New projects are always subject to operational and financial setbacks, even shortly before commissioning. Especially the projects located in higher risk regions may be subject to longer delays. Despite the fact that CRU has been conservative in our forecasts, delays are always possible. **Technical challenges at HPAL operations.** There has been evidence that major HPAL operations are successfully commissioning. However, this kind of operations has historically experienced technical challenges that should not be disregarded when conducting a high and low case scenario analysis. ###### Downside risks to the price outlook **Weaker than anticipated industrial production activity.** Considering the advanced level of downside macroeconomic risks, especially in industrialised countries, deterioration in industrial activity will have an impact on cobalt consumption. For instance, a weaker than expected world industrial activity will affect the market for cemented carbides as demand from the automotive, steel and shipbuilding industries will soften. ###### **Unfavourable technology developments that trigger substitution of cobalt or lower intensity of** **use.** Miniaturisation trends in end-use markets will affect cobalt consumption. This is very important in high-end devices that need to be lighter and smaller over time. The most critical end-use sector is lithium ion rechargeable batteries. **Refined cobalt production stronger compared to CRU’s expectations.** CRU has taken a conservative approach to forecasting refined cobalt production. If the actual production level is higher than what we project, the refined cobalt market will exhibit a higher surplus. Our conservative forecasting approach applies both to large and small scale operations. **Aggressive development of new projects.** If that takes place it will affect mainly the long-run outlook, considering the time needed to develop new projects. Lately, in view of the growing consumption volume of cobalt, as well as its contribution to high-end technologies, there has been a growing interest from investment groups to be involved in the cobalt industry. CRU International Limited confidential The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 Chapter 1 14 ##### 1. Uses of cobalt Cobalt is a ferromagnetic, silver white, hard, lustrous element. Its physical properties are similar to the ones of iron and nickel. Like iron, it can be magnetised. Cobalt is active chemically and can form many compounds. It is stable in air and unaffected by water; however, it can be slowly attacked by dilute acids. Cobalt-based blue pigments have been used since ancient times for jewellery and paints, and to create a distinctive blue tint to glass. CRU’s cobalt demand analysis is based on a real consumption methodology. Our demand estimates are expressed on a cobalt contained basis. We have identified 33 end-use sectors for cobalt, as presented in Table 1.1. For each end-use sector we analyse its market size and then take into consideration its cobalt-specific intensity of use to estimate real cobalt consumption. By following this methodology we avoid the potential problem due to changes in inventory levels that an apparent consumption based methodology would generate. In fact, an apparent consumption methodology in the case of cobalt would be questionable due to the complexity of trade flows as well as misclassifications in trade codes. A high-level segmentation of refined cobalt consumption is between the chemical and the metallurgical sectors. In the chemical sector, we conduct analysis on the following cobalt products: acetate, carbonate, chloride, hydroxide, oxide, nitrate, sulphate, and organics (carboxylates). The most important by market size is the lithium cobalt oxide, which is used

in lithium ion battery cathodes.  The material is composed of cobalt oxide layers in which the lithium is intercalated.  During discharging, the lithium intercalated between the layers is set free as lithium ion.  This is widely used in the batteries of electronic devices. 

In the metallurgical sector, the distinct properties of cobalt fulfil the requirements of a number of end-use sectors where strength, high ware resistance and high temperature resistance are demanded.  The cemented carbide sector is an important one for cobalt.  Cemented carbides are composed of a metal matrix composite where carbide particles act as the aggregate and a metallic binder serves as the matrix.  This solution is used in machining tough materials such as carbon steel or stainless steel, as well as in situations where other tools would ware. Additionally, the aerospace industry is an important market for cobalt.  Indeed, performance in hot corrosion and resistance, along with reasonable weldability, means that cobalt alloys are favoured in various rotating parts for jet engines, particularly fan blades. 

As analysed in this chapter, cobalt is consumed by high-end markets.  Despite cobalt’s use by cutting edge industries, final consumers are not aware of its contribution to economic and industrial growth.  Rarely does a final consumer know that cobalt is an essential element in the battery of smartphones, prosthetics or aircraft engines.  The European Commission has identified cobalt as one of the 14 economically important raw materials.  From a demand point of view, cobalt contributes to economic growth of developing regions.  In addition, it is central to the emergence of new technologies and products.

##### 2. Demand for cobalt in 2011 

This section refers to Table 1.1.  We estimate that world refined cobalt consumption amounted to 77,015 tonnes in 2011.  The figure represented a 5.9% year-on-year increase from the previous year.  This rate was a deceleration from 13.9% growth registered in 2010; this is attributed first to a return to more sustainable demand growth rates after the rebound from the global financial crisis, and second to a slowdown in the global recovery in 2011 attributed to a number of macroeconomic and other factors.  CRU believes that cobalt demand growth is healthy and comfortably outperforms advances in the global industrial production (IP) index, which captures a broad range of economic activity.  In 2011, world IP rose by 4.8%; the fact that cobalt consumption growth outperformed the general IP index is backed by cobalt’s contribution to growing end-use markets, which are less vulnerable to the current macroeconomic downside risks. 

Looking at long-term consumption trends, refined cobalt demand in 2011 was up by 90% when compared to 2000 levels.  Refined cobalt consumption grew at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.0% in 2000-2011, which

includes a modest contraction of 0.5% year-on-year in 2009. 

###### 2.1 Cobalt use in chemical sectors 

Refined cobalt consumption in chemical forms reached 44,150 tonnes in 2011, a 6.3% increase from 2010.  Demand for cobalt in chemical forms made 57% of total refined consumption in 2011.  Chemical cobalt consumption advanced at a CAGR of 8.2% in 2000-2011, contributing significantly to the expansion of the total cobalt market. 

Cobalt oxide used in lithium ion battery cells for electronic devices accounted for 53% of chemical consumption in 2011.  This particular end-use accounted for 30% of total (chemical and metallurgical) refined cobalt consumption in 2011.  Cobalt oxide in lithium ion batteries registered a 16.3% CAGR in 2000-2011, by far the strongest of any other large-sized end-use sector.  The most important final products we have taken into consideration in our analysis are mobile phones and laptops.  The world market for mobile phones amounted to 1.47 billion units in 2011; 32% of this figure was smartphones while 68% standard (non-smartphone) mobile phones.  CRU believes that cobalt intensity of use in smartphones amounted to an average of 5.9 grams per unit, while that of standard mobile phones 3.5 grams per unit.  When estimating consumption in the long-run we incorporate the increasing market share of smartphones as well as the effects of final product miniaturisation. 

Demand for cobalt acetate rose by 6.1% year-on-year to 4,474 tonnes in 2011.  This is an important market for cobalt, which expanded at a CAGR of 6.8% in 2000-2011.  The principal end-use of cobalt acetate is the manufacture of PET, which is mainly used to produce polyester fibres for synthetic textiles, packaging, and bottles.  Clean plastic bottles in particular have seen strong growth, supported by the increase in the sales of bottled water and soft/energy drinks. Cobalt acetate is used as a catalyst.

The figure increased by 5.3% from the previous year and 51% from 2000. Demand from metallurgical sectors rose at a CAGR of 3.8% in 2000-2011. The demand growth in metallurgical sectors was slower compared to that in chemical sectors. We estimate that cemented carbides made 6,652 tonnes of refined cobalt consumption in 2011. Cobalt consumption by this end-use sector rose by 5.0% from the previous year. It is a growing market, having seen a CAGR of 6.3% in 2000-2011. Sumitomo Electric Industries commented that demand in this market has been increasing on a global scale due to economic development and growing automobile production especially in emerging regions. Cemented carbides are essential for machining all kinds of mechanical parts in the automotive, steel, shipbuilding and IT industries. Sandvik estimated that the average annual growth rate in this segment has been 4-5%. Interestingly, this is consistent with our view, which suggests that cobalt demand from the cemented carbide and diamond tool markets advanced at a CAGR of 4.5% in 2000-2011. Demand for superalloys used in aircraft engine rotating parts saw a 7.3% year-on-year growth to 4,545 tonnes in 2011. The civil aerospace business of Rolls-Royce delivered 962 engines in 2011, an increase of 13.7% year-on-year. The defence aerospace business of the same engine manufacturer reported a 14.6% year-on-year increase to 814 deliveries in 2011. In addition, Boeing said that it expects to deliver 585-600 commercial aircraft in 2012, an increase of 22.625.8% year-on-year. Considering the time lag between cobalt use in engine building and final aircraft delivery, the above means that cobalt consumption growth by this end-use sector was robust in 2011. Cobalt in superalloys used in other engineering sectors reached an estimated 5,215 tonnes in 2011. The figure was up by 4.6% from the previous year. The long term regional consumption development is central to the analysis of the cobalt market. Looking at changes in 2000-2011 allows us to derive concrete conclusions. T

his period has seen aggressive growth in the consumption of emerging economies, production migration of end-use sectors, advances in technology, socio-economic development on a global basis, as well as the global financial crisis.  Therefore, it would be interesting to study these developments from a cobalt consumption standpoint. 

As in the analysis of every commodity, the most striking development is the emergence of China as the largest cobalt consumer in the world.  Refined cobalt consumption in China rose from 3,780 tonnes in 2000 to 27,053 tonnes in 2011.  This represents a CAGR of 19.6%, the fastest of any other region or country.  In terms of world percentage share, Chinese cobalt consumption surged from 9.3% in 2000 to 35.1% in 2011.  This has mainly been triggered by soaring cobalt oxide consumption by domestic lithium ion battery makers.  The manufacture of batteries has traditionally been an Asian business, which used to take place in the past primarily in North East Asia.  That used to serve the local electronics supply chains. 

Therefore, as these supply chains migrated to China, battery production moved there too. Despite robust growth in the Chinese share of refined cobalt consumption, this is still less than other major industrial metals that CRU covers.  For instance, the Chinese share of refined copper consumption in 2011was 39.6%, while that of primary aluminium 43.1%.  This is attributed to the fact that despite the strong growth by chemical sectors in China, the metallurgical sectors have not registered a similar one.  Indeed, the Chinese consumption share of world metallurgical demand rose from 10.7% in 2000 to 23.6% in 2011.  This is because China has not benefited yet from the strong cobalt demand growth by the aerospace industry and advanced engineering.  We assume that commercial aircraft engine manufacturing in China will commence in 2016, therefore cobalt consumption is anticipated to start a year earlier. 

The Rest of Asia saw the second fastest demand growth between 2000 and 2011.  Cobalt consumption registered a CAGR of 5.0% to 21,137 tonnes in 2011.  This region has exhibited a different growth pattern compared to China, exhibiting signs of a mature market.  In our demand model, this region mainly consists of Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.  On the one hand the Rest of Asia has benefited from strong demand from the lithium ion battery cell segment, on the other hand it has suffered due to production migration of this sector to China.

The reason that the chemical sector became so important in the cobalt market is the growth in lithium ion cell batteries. We estimate that this market amounted to 23,434 tonnes of cobalt in 2011. China accounted for 59% of that volume, followed by the Rest of Asia with 40% and the USA with 1%. While battery production mainly takes place in China, there is still significant production in North East Asia. Cobalt consumed by lithium ion batteries for electronic devices accounted for 30.4% of total world refined consumption. A growing segment for cobalt that has not seen its full potential yet is electric vehicles (EV) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEV). So far, EV/HEV have mainly been using nickel metal hydride and nickel cadmium batteries, which consume cobalt hydroxide. CRU estimates that cobalt hydroxide used by batteries in EV/HEV reached 1,824 tonnes in 2011. The Rest of Asia accounted for 73% of that volume which supplies final products, such as the Toyota Prius. Even though lithium ion batteries have started supplying the EV/HEV segment, their share was still small, hence using only an estimated 332 tonnes on a world level in 2011. World demand for cobalt acetate, which is principally used in the production of PET, totalled 4,474 tonnes in 2011. Even though it is consumed in all regions, the Rest of Asia accounted for 41% of the world total cobalt acetate consumption. Th

is is attributed to large PET production volumes especially in South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, India, and Indonesia. Despite significant imports of PET, the USA remains a major producer of this commodity. US acetate consumption was 990 tonnes in 2011. Indeed, demand for acetate accounted for 26.3% of total US cobalt chemical consumption in 2011. Cobalt acetate is consumed around the world due to the fact that production of PET is a global business. Demand from metallurgical sectors made 42.7% of total refined cobalt consumption in 2011. Out of total metallurgical demand, the USA and Western Europe accounted for 56.6%. Cobalt in superalloys used in aircraft engines totalled 4,545 tonnes in 2011, which was almost equally distributed between the USA and Western Europe. We assume that, at the moment, commercial large-scale production of aircraft engines takes place only in the above regions. Cobalt consumption in cemented carbides and diamond tools reached 8,051 tonnes in 2011. Historically, this is one of the most important metallurgical sectors of cobalt. Its development originated in Germany in the 1920s; it was introduced in the USA shortly afterwards and subsequent development occurred in other industrialised countries. In 2011, the USA, China, the Rest of Asia, and Western Europe jointly accounted for 7,647 tonnes or 95% of cobalt used in carbides and diamond tools on a world level. Within the field of engineering materials, cemented carbides have a crucial role as they combine high hardness and strength with good toughness within a good property range. However, production requires advanced engineering. This usually happens when an established manufacturer sets up subsidiaries or partnerships in industrialising regions. Examples include Japan’s Sumitomo Electric Industries and Mitsubishi Materials, which have expanded their cemented carbide operations in China and other industrialising countries in Asia. CRU International Limited confidential The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 Chapter 1 28 ##### 5. Forecast demand for cobalt This section refers to Table 1.4. CRU projects that demand for refined cobalt will rise by 5.9% year-on-year to 81,554 tonnes in 2012. We believe that despite the prevailing macroeconomic challenges, robust growth of end-use sectors will continue to support cobalt consumption. Cobalt consumption by chemical end-use sectors is predicted to expand by 7.2% to 47,310 tonnes in 2012. That will correspond to 58% of total cobalt demand, up from 57% in 2011. Demand from metallurgical sectors is expected to increase by 4.2% to 34,245 tonnes in 2012. Looking ahead, we anticipate that the global refined cobalt market will amount to 113,416 tonnes in 2017. This represents a CAGR of 6.8% in 2012-2017. CRU expects that world cobalt consumption will accelerate in 2013-2015, as the world economy recovers from the current slowdown. This projection is consistent with CRU’s economic and industrial outlook. We expect that cobalt consumption growth will accelerate to 6.9%, 7.1%, and 7.8% year-on-year in 2013-2015. This is supported by a stronger industrial production outlook, and market-specific trends in cobalt demand. We anticipate that cobalt demand growth will decelerate to 6.4% and 5.9% year-on-year in 2016-2017, converging to the long-term consumption growth rate. ##### 1. Cobalt reserve base 

Cobalt is usually found in low concentrations and is extracted primarily as a by- or co-product of mining for other metals, mainly nickel and copper. The Cobalt Development Institute estimated that in 2011 55% of cobalt production came from nickel mining, 35% from the mining of copper and other minerals and 10% from primary cobalt sources. 

Cobalt is widely scattered in the earth‟s crust and a concentration can be found in potentially exploitable quantities in several countries in the world. Significant resources of cobalt are also present in the deep-sea nodules and crusts which occur in the Mid-Pacific, although these are not economically viable with current technology and economic conditions. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), as much as 1 billion tons of hypothetical and speculative cobalt resources may exist in manganese nodules and crusts on the ocean floor. 

Economic c

oncentrations of cobalt can be found in three different geological settings. The first is in sediment hosted, which can be found in the African Copper Belt, the world‟s most important cobalt source. The second is hydrothermal and volcanogenic, for example at Bou Azzer in Morocco. The third geological setting is magmatic sulphide and related laterite deposits, which can be found in Cuba, New Caledonia, Australia and Russia. 

###### 1.1 Conventional assessments 

Through the years, geologists, mining engineers and other specialists operating in the minerals field have used various terms to describe and classify cobalt mineral reserves and resources. Some of these terms have gained wide use and acceptance, although they are not always used with precisely the same meaning. 

We use the definition of resources and reserves by the USGS which states that a cobalt resource is a concentration of naturally occurring solid material most often within the Earth‟s crust in such form and amount that economic extraction of a commodity from the concentration can be potentially feasible. The resource should meet specified minimum physical and chemical criteria in order to be mined viably in regards to grade, quality, thickness and depth. The reserve, however, is considered to be a demonstrated (measured plus indicated) part of the resource which could be economically extracted or produced at the time of determination. 

Cobalt sources have changed over history, from Norway, Sweden, Hungary and Germany to the dependence on the African Copper Belt. In the last decade, sources have diversified with increasing amounts coming from nickel and copper ores as well as recycled scrap and cobalt containing intermediates. 

The USGS estimated that the physically available resource and reserve base for cobalt worldwide was 15.2 million tonnes and 7.7 million tonnes respectively in 2011. The vast majority of these resources are situated in nickel-bearing laterite deposits, with most of the rest occurring in nickel-copper sulphide deposits hosted in mafic and ultramafic rocks in Australia, Canada, and Russia, and in the sedimentary copper deposits of Congo (Kinshasa) and Zambia.

##### 2. Mine production 

After cobalt resources and reserves, the next stage in the production of refined cobalt is _mine production._ In detail, cobalt production is dependent on ore and concentrates from many sources, some of which are relatively obscure.  There are several small nickel mines for example in Australia that produce nickel concentrates that contain cobalt which are shipped overseas for refining in Canada, Finland and China. Similarly, operations in Botswana, Brazil and Canada send mainly nickel concentrates containing cobalt to major smelting and refining operations in their respective countries. We have therefore listed the operations where cobalt is mined in Table 2.3 overleaf. We have identified 51 operations where cobalt ore is mined and show where the respective ores and concentrates are processed. 

The objective in our tracking of cobalt production at the mine level has been to provide a check on our refined production numbers and particularly to reconcile the volumes of material imported by China and Finland where major volumes of refined metal and chemicals are produced. 

As identified in Table 2.3, mined production was nearly 73,000 tonnes of contained cobalt in 2009. This increased by nearly 25% year-on-year to just over 90,000 tonnes in 2010 and a further 8% to 97,000 tonnes in 2011. 

The largest source of mined cobalt production over this period has been the African Copper Belt, with the DRC and Zambia supplying over 60% of this material (59,000 tonnes of cobalt contained). We have identified 14 operations in the DRC, which collectively produced 53,300 tonnes of cobalt in ores and concentrates in 2011. Operations in Russia, Cuba, Australia and Canada contributed a further 19,000 tonnes of contained cobalt during the period while the lateritic deposits in the Pacific found in Indonesia, New Caledonia and the Philippines supplied the bulk of the remainder. 

The operations in the African Copper Belt are extremely significant as they are probably going to be the source of choice for increasing supply in the longer term, particularly to China. The 14 operations currently producing ores and concentrates in the DRC reflect the abundance of deposits and the relative ease in establishing a mine with a heavy media separating plant that can produce concentrates. Some of these operations such as Kov, Kamoto and Tenke Fungurume are large scale integrated mine and metallurgical facilities but nevertheless, it is not inconceivable that future mining operations in the DRC could support production of a further 30-40,000 tonnes of cobalt in the long-term.

Cobalt refined production in 2011 In spite of well anticipated and often substantial production cuts at leading refined producers around the world last year, such as Katanga Mining in the DRC, primary cobalt production rose again emphatically overall to 78,296 tonnes, gaining 9.5%. In 2011, output of cobalt specialty products and chemicals rose most strongly; by 11.8% to 45,476 tonnes. This segment of the market accounted for a 58% share of total primary output, up from 57% in 2010. Interestingly, China‟s production share of specialty products fell last year, largely because of a large decline at leading operations Zhejiang Huayou and Jinchuan, both of whom who had been unwilling, given slackening market fundamentals, to maintain full capacity as in 2010. Indeed Huayou, a 6,000 tpy chemicals producer by capacity, produced 4,000 tonnes last year, down from 5,800 tonnes in 2010; a level supported by an excess of raw material the company had been keen to draw down. Overall, however, specialty production in China still rose impressively to 29,839 tonnes last year or 66% of the global total, supported by Huayou‟s neighbour Galico, Ganzhou Hengsheng Umicore and some smaller facilities. The largest growth, however, came from outside of China, for example India, albeit from a low starting point, but also the Yabulu refinery in Australia, which had another strong growth year in reaching 2,631 tonnes up from 2,189 tonnes in 2010. On the metal producing side, Katanga Mining – the third largest metal producer in 2010 with the reported potential to become number one – was not alone in recording a decline, though the 29.2% retreat to just 2,433 tonnes was the largest of all major producers. While the company continued to be impacted by an oversupplied market, lower cobalt head grades and electricity constraints were major factors in last year‟s decline. Electricity constraints affected various operations last year, particularly in the final quarter. In Norway, meanwhile, Xstrata recorded a 4.4% decline of their high

grade cobalt refined at Nikkelverk – a 5,200 tpy processor – though they remained fourth largest producer globally by exceeding 3,000 tonnes. Nevertheless last year was another characterised by solid advances in the metal producing sector overall. The 6.4% gain to 32,820 tonnes was supported in particular by Vale‟s so-called “return to normalcy” in Sudbury, Canada following a lengthy strike. This took production from 1,065 tonnes to 2,675 tonnes (including 1,585 tonnes refined in Voisey Bay). This ensured Vale became the fifth largest producer overall. Jinchuan, meanwhile, the fifth largest metal producer in 2010, moved up the leader board to third, with 3,143 tonnes and the largest producers Chambishi Metals and ICCI (50% owned by Sherritt through the Moa Joint Venture) surged to an estimated 4,856 tonnes and 3,854 tonnes respectively. ###### 7.1 Estimates of specific cobalt production costs 

Our estimates of cobalt production costs for by-product cobalt have come from the CRU inhouse copper and nickel production cost models. Virtually all of by-product cobalt is produced in the nickel refineries and the integrated metal producers and collectively, this represents the largest volume of refined cobalt production. 

We have focused exclusively on the specific costs of producing cobalt at these operations. Generally speaking this has involved assessing the costs in the purification of the cobalt leach liquor and the electro-winning of cobalt metal or the case of the Sherritt process, the hydrometallurgical precipitation, sintering and briquetting of the metal. 

Our cost estimates have been prepared from a bottom-up approach, assessing the costs of power, labour and consumables for the purification and electro-winning or briquetting stages. We have also estimated the costs of delivering the cobalt produced into the key markets of the We

stern Hemisphere and China where appropriate. 

Where we have relevant information, we have included the costs of maintenance, sustaining and working capital. The operations where we have included these costs are generally the integrated metal producers where we have assembled detailed cost profiles in the CRU copper and nickel cost models. In the nickel refineries, where cobalt is produced at a very late stage in the refining process, we have assumed that these costs would be absorbed by the main metal, nickel. 

For operations where cobalt is the main product, we have taken typical, mining, milling, smelting and refining costs for the operations involved. This has involved using appropriate country input parameters for power, labour and consumables and modelling the specific operation. For example, the _OMG Big Hill_ operation and the _Chambishi Cosac_ plant are both

In our assessment of the Chinese processing operations, we have looked at the three types of cobalt raw materials imported into China at present: alliage blanc, cobalt concentrates and hydro metallurgical intermediates. 

We have used our estimated cobalt contents of these materials, recovery rates and the current pricing practices for these materials. For example, we have assumed that in the case of cobalt concentrates, they contain 6% cobalt, recovery is 75% and payment is made at 60% of the metal price. For hydrometallurgical intermediates such as crude carbonate and hydroxide, cobalt content is much higher at 25%, recovery is also better at 85% and price paid is 70% of the metal price. We have also estimated overland freight costs out of the DRC, ocean freight and internal Chinese freight charges in order to assess the full costs of these materials before they are leached and converted to chemicals. 

In assessing the costs of delivering refined cobalt to market, we have continued to use the “realisation cost” estimates from our cost models. Realisation costs include freight charges from the production centre into a major market, marketing and sales costs and interest on the cost of the pipeline that is required to be established for delivery. Where a crude intermediate is produced, our approach assumes that either a refining _cost_ or a refining _charge_ will need to be estimated in order to fully quantify the realisations costs. 

In the case of the OMG Big Hill operation, alliage blanc is sent to the company‟s operations in Finland for further processing. In this case we assume the material attracts a _refining cost_ as part of the realisations costs. Similarly, the crude carbonate produced at the Ruashi operation in the DRC (recently purchased by Jinchuan) incurs

a refining cost as well, as this material will be processed at the Jinchuan plant in China. However, in the case of the crude hydroxide produced by Tenke Fungurume, we assume that this incurs a _refining charge_ as this is effectively sold to a third party. In estimating the refining charge we have used current tolling tariffs. On this question of refining charges and costs, we have assumed that the specific costs of producing cobalt from mixed nickel cobalt intermediates is zero until the last stage of refining. Prices are obtained from telephone surveys with traders and consumers in Europe and North America. Also in the USA, the US Defence Logistics Agency‟s (DLA) Strategic Materials Directorate had been selling cobalt from its stockpile since 1993, which at the time amounted to 52m pounds, with the sales price published after each transaction. DLA sales historically played a role in the price discovery process, but as stocks have diminished are now much less relevant, with only a handful of small transactions concluded each year depending on business conditions. In the 2009 financial year, for example, only 412,320 lbs were sold for just over $6.8m. No sales have taken place since 2009. After 2000, several other price reporting systems emerged. The Cobalt Open Sales System (COSS) was an internet trading platform originally developed by WMC Resources for the sales of its 99.8% cobalt cathode, produced at Falconbridge‟s Nikkelverk refine

ry. BHP Billiton continued this system after the takeover of WMC. In addition to BHP Billiton, other producers, notably Norilsk and Jinchuan, provided quotations for their cobalt products via websites. Norilsk, in common with the BHP COSS site, also provided information on prices and volumes from recent transactions. As a further development of this type of trading system, Metal Bulletin introduced a Metal Price Watch system in 2004 where buyers and sellers are matched on an open auction system. These prices now form the basis of MB cobalt price quotations. However, two of these price information sources have now disappeared. In August 2008, Norilsk announced it would no longer publish a cobalt price, saying this was giving too much information away to rivals. Furthermore, BHP decided in January 2009 to suspend the publication of the COSS price and the company now states it will direct market all of its cobalt production. It is purely a cashsettled contract, but does give participants in the physical market the possibility of hedging price risk. ###### 2.1 Prices prior to 1990 Before 1979, all cobalt metal was sold at the producer list price. Producers sold their cobalt in line with the Union Miniиre or, as it later became, the Gйcamines (DRC) price. The so-called “freemarket price” began to emerge between 1978 and 1980, when a supply crisis loosened the producers‟ dominance of the pricing system. During the early 1980s, the free market broadly followed the producer price. In 1984, ZCCM and Gйcamines made a bid to recover their price leadership position by restricting supplies in order to keep the price within agreed levels (US$11.45 to US$11.70/lb). At that time, supply and demand were more or less in balan

ce. 

During 1985, the impact of capacity expansions resulted in production growing much faster than supply and, by the final quarter, stocks had grown to high levels.  Furthermore, the freemarket was well supplied through barter deals and producers were selling openly to traders in order to move stocks.  The result was a price fall from around US$11 to US$6/lb. 

At that time, Gйcamines held a key position as the swing supplier.  At times of high demand they could meet the additional requirements by selling from their stocks.  Conversely, at times of weak demand, Gйcamines would stockpile material while their competitors reduced prices to capture marginal market share and ensure they sold their full production.  So, when Gйcamines opted to sell more material to the market under these conditions in an attempt to capture market share, the price fell rapidly.  As prices were still above production costs and cobalt was generally regarded as a by-product, there was little resistance to these falling prices.  Only when Gйcamines held prices fixed in 1986-87 did the price begin to stabilise.

During 1987-90, Gйcamines began to look at strategies to maximise its revenues from cobalt. They concluded that to do this in a sustainable way would require a steady increase in cobalt consumption over time.  Furthermore, it concluded that this could only be achieved by ensuring stable pricing and secure supplies.  Subsequently, the producer price was increased gradually in three iterative steps, with the free market price generally rising in anticipation of these announcements.  Meanwhile, Gйcamines also sought to establish long-term contracts with consumers in an attempt to persuade them that supplies would be secure and prices would be fixed.  To encourage this, the company offered discounts of up to 10% on large tonnages. However, they failed to provide firm guarantees on price structure. 

As a result, many small and medium-sized consumers preferred to source their material from other producers and purchase at least part of their requirements from traders, in order to manage their exposure to a single supplier.  It was only the large consumers, who purchased more than 100 tonnes of cobalt per year, which accepted the contract terms with Gйcamines in order to guarantee their supplies. 

###### 2.2 Cobalt prices in 1991-2006 

The price of cobalt remained at a relatively low and stable level for the latter years in the 1980s. However by mid-way through 1990 Gйcamines began to experience production difficulties.  In June 1991, its Kamoto mine, which was an important source of cobalt-rich ore, suffered a serious collapse and production at this location fell to a third of previous levels.  This was compounded by the rapidly deteriorating political situation in the DRC (then Zaire).  Consumers with long-term contracts began to experience delays in delivery.  The market becam

e rife with uncertainty.  Doubt was expressed in the media about Gйcamines' ability to continue to supply cobalt in the long-term. 

Against the backdrop of these supply disruptions the producer price became meaningless and, during 1991, the Zambians saw an opportunity to increase their prices by selling through traders at the freemarket price.  Meanwhile, Gйcamines was struggling to meet its supply contracts.  As a result, all supplies of metal were being priced at freemarket prices, which reached US$30/lb during the early part of 1992, equivalent to a 4-fold increase in little over a year.  At the end of 1991, the African producers followed the freemarket price, setting the producer price at US$25/lb. 

Meanwhile, there emerged an increased availability of supplies of Russian cobalt.  Russian material was supplied in ingot form and at a lower grade of purity; 99.3% cobalt compared with 99.8% for Grade "A" cathode.  Initially, many consumers were unwilling to take this material as they found the 3kg to 5kg ingots much more difficult to handle than granules or cut cathode. 

The continued supply of material from the DRC and Zambia, coupled with increased availability of Russian cobalt, led to a sustained decline in cobalt prices.  During June 1992, the freemarket price fell below the producer price and continued falling well into the third quarter of 1993.  The African producers were uncertain how best to respond.  Faced with a need to keep prices at US$25/lb in order to maintain revenue and the fear of a rapid decline in the metal price similar to that seen in 1985-86, they decided to maintain a higher producer price. 

The result was that Gйcamines and ZCCM lost significant market share to the freemarket. Combined, stocks held by the two companies approached 9,000 tonnes by November 1992.

They decided to reduce the producer price to US$18/lb, the level of the freemarket at that time. Both companies began to sell material, but there were frequent reports of sales at much lower prices to traders and large consumers as the free market price became dominant again. Subsequently, Zambia introduced a cobalt reference price of US$21/lb in consultation with Gйcamines in April 1994, but its influence was negligible in the market.  In February 1995, this reference price was raised to US$27.50. 

The main purpose of this reference price was to set a level at which the African producers could sell their metal committed on long-term contracts.  However, since May 1996 this price has been well above the freemarket price and as supply constraints have been limited, this price quotation has been largely irrelevant.  For this reason it is no longer quoted. 

Historically, cobalt prices have been characterised by strong volatility, with the peaks and troughs seen over the past 18 years correlating with certain key events.  The peak of over US$30/lb in 1991 was caused by supp

ly problems from DRC that followed the mine collapse at Kamoto that year and a serious civil disturbance in Katanga Province, where the Gйcamines facilities are located. The subsequent trough (US$10/lb) in 1992 reflected a correction in purchasing patterns, partly as a result of high prices and partly because consumers had built up large inventories in the preceding months as they rushed to secure available supply. The next significant peak, in 1996, was the result of steadily increasing demand in a market where supply was tight. This was a period when trading activity was at its most influential. Further to that, prices dropped steadily as more supplies became available. The sharp downward spike in prices in January 1999 to US$7/lb was precipitated by sales of cobalt stock held by ZCCM to a leading trader. There were accusations of price manipulation over this transaction. However the price did not stay at that level for long and returned quite rapidly to over US$20/lb by mid-1999. Subsequently, increased supply arising from investments made during the high prices in the period 1994-96 led to overcapacity and prices drifted back towards US$7/lb by November 2001. Prices began to rise sharply again in 2003-04 as demand showed significant growth. This stemmed from the vast increase in the amount of rechargeable battery cells required to meet the rapidly growing mobile phone and portable computer markets, and the emergence of China as a major consumer nation. From a peak in early 2004, the price fell gradually through 2004 and 2005, reaching a low point of US$12.50 in February 2006. The fall occurred mainly as a result of a build-up of battery cell inventories and reduced buying from this sector coupled with some aggressive selling by one of the producers. From February 2006 the price rose steadily again, accelerating sharply during the northern hemisphere winter to over US$25/lb in December 2006. Sentiment turned abruptly bullish in November 2006, following the announcement that Norilsk would in the future (from March 2007) sell its cobalt solely to OM Group, effectively withdrawing a significant supply of cobalt from the open marketplace. The cobalt price outlook – long-term ###### 6.1 The long-term price outlook methodology This section summarises CRU‟s approach to forecasting long-term cobalt prices. Essentially, it follows CRU‟s development of the concept that long-run commodity prices are driven by the long-run marginal cost of production (LRMC), as well as the industry response to this cost of production by the behaviour of marginal producers and the creation of new capacity. In the case of cobalt, developing this concept is more complicated than most other commodities and metals because it is pr

oduced in different forms and it is mainly a by-product of copper and nickel, which are more significant metals in terms of volume. 

###### 6.2 The long-term market balance 

Our supply and demand analysis suggests that there is going to be a deficit in the refined cobalt market in the long-run.  This immediately implies that cobalt prices will increase in order to attract the development of new projects.  With refined demand expected to grow at a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022, sufficient supply will be needed to meet consumption needs.  Our supply and demand balance shows that the refined market will exhibit a deficit of 28,840 tonnes in 2022.  We project that the raw material market will be balanced in 2022 but this is only to meet the refined production forecast we present in Chapter 2, rather than world consumption needs. Within the cobalt feed supply analysis, we have assumed that there will be an increase in the supply of concentrates from the DRC in order to meet the cobalt feed needs, in particular those for Chinese processors.  That may be affected by the DRC government restricting exports of concentrate in favour of intermediate products and capture domestically the value added. 

The fact that the raw material market appears to be balanced in 2022 does not mean that there will be enough cobalt units to meet refined demand needs.  This is because the refined market will be in deficit, meaning that new processing capacity will be needed, especially in order to produce chemical products.  The refined supply and demand analysis conducted in Chapter 1 and 2 shows that the chemical market will be increasingly tighter in the future, and that should trigger expansions or new projects.  We believe that this new capacity, in the form of expansions or new projects, will be most likely located in China in order to satisfy soaring demand from regional chemical end-use sectors. 

The projected refined market deficit in 2022 is an indication of the need of the future cobalt needed at a refined level, on top of current production.  These material requirements are expressed in cobalt contained terms at a refined level; they provide a measure of the quantity of cobalt units needed in the supply chain in 2022. ###### 2.1 The Americas: USA suffers summer doldrums again 

**The indications are that the USA is experiencing its third bout of summer softness in a row.** In recent weeks **first quarter GDP growth** was revised down from 2.2% annualised to **1.9%** , thanks to changes in the estimates of the contributions made by trade, stocks and public spending.   High frequency data suggests that the **second quarter’s performance won’t be much different** .  We have it at 2.2% annualised, but **the risks are that it could come in** 

**around 20 basis points lower.  For an economy which should be able to grow by 2.5% on trend, and somewhat above that during the recovery phase of its cycle, this is soft.** 

Last year the key problem was the dampening effects on spending caused by high oil prices. **This year the problem is mainly to do with the Eurozone’s downswing, and with the debilitating effects of the uncertainty emanating from the Eurozone on confidence.** One positive consequence is that inflation is falling back, which should support real spending in the second half of 2012.  As a result we’ve only shaved 10 basis points off our growth forecast for this year, trimming it to 2.2%.  The strong affinity to muddling through shown by policy makers in the Eurozone leads us to think that uncertainty will remain a dominant feature of the outlook for some time yet,  however, and the dampening effect this will have on confidence has led us to trim 10-20 basis points off our US growth forecasts through to 2016 as well. 

**The evidence of deceleration is widespread.** Industrial production eased down by 0.1% m- o-m in May, led by a broad-based 0.4% drop in manufacturing output.  In part this was payback for the unusual strength of production in the first quarter.  But on trend manufacturing has decelerated from double digit growth in the New Year to low single-digit growth now.  Further deceleration is likely: bookings for factory goods dropped in April, by 0.6% m-o-m for the third time in four months. 

**The USA’s dividend from rebalancing towards its external sector is diminishing as the crisis in the Eurozone intensifies.** This isn’t because of a serious loss of competitiveness, which is still high, although it’s being eroded at the margins by the weakening €, but because of sharp absolute falls in demand and heightened uncertainty.   In April the 0.8% m-o-m fall back in exports was concentrated in capital goods and industrial supplies and materials.  The main weak spot in the USA’s markets was Europe, where demand for American goods has slumped dramatically on an annualised basis, from almost 15% growth in August 2011 to a contraction of almost 5% in April.  In contrast exports to China are still rising.

What might a Eurozone crash look like? Meanwhile the banking sectors in the exiting countries and in the surviving rump of the Eurozone would suffer heavy losses and tighten credit standards dramatically.  These losses would imply the socialisation of significant additional debt.
